APPROACH TO HYPOTHERMIA 
 
 
 
 
 
DEFINITION 
Core temperature of ≤35°C for non-trauma patients 
Core Temperature of ≤36°C for trauma patients 
 
Swiss 
Staging 
Clinical Features 
Typical 
Temperature 
I 
Conscious, shivering 
32 – 35°C 
II 
Impaired consciousness, not 
shivering 
28 – 32°C 
III 
Unconscious, not shivering, 
vital signs present 
24 – 28°C 
IV 
Vital signs absent 
< 24°C 
 
The preferred site to measure core temperature in severely 
hypothermic patients is the lower third of the oesophagus as 
this most closely approximates cardiac temperature. If this is 
unavailable or the patient is not intubated, a RECTAL PROBE is 
acceptable but is less accurate and will lag behind true cardiac 
temperature with rewarming. 
 
TREAT HYPOTHERMIA AGGRESIVELY  
ALL OTHER INTERVENTIONS ARE LIKELY TO FAIL 
 
https://emergencymedicinecases.com/accidental-hypothermia-cardiac-arrest/ 
 
ED MANAGEMENT  
 
Stage 
Management 
I 
Warm environment & clothing, warm sweet drinks & active movement 
 
II 
Cardiac monitoring, careful movement of patient to avoid arrhythmias, full-body 
insulation, active external rewarming & minimally invasive rewarming (warm 
environment, electrical, or forced-air heating blankets; warm parenteral fluids) , 
correct hypoglycaemia 
 
III 
 Same as hypothermia Stage II with airway management as indicated 
PLUS 
 Central active warming 
• 
warm IV fluids (42°C)  (only give if need fluids, prevents cooling rather 
than promotes warming)  
• 
body cavity lavage with 40°C fluid e.g., gastric, bladder, right-sided 
thoracic lavage (increases by 3-6°C/hr) 
• 
make sure patient is intubated before attempting gastric lavage 
• 
Bladder lavage: 
o warm up fluid in microwave if needed make sure  not too hot! 
o empty the bladder after urinary catheter insertion 
o  connect IV giving set to urinary catheter 
o Infuse ±500ml of warm fluid 
o Close the drip and wait for 10mins 
o Empty the bladder 
o Repeat until core temperature improves 
• 
Renal replacement therapy 
• 
ECMO/ bypass (increase by 9-18°C/h) 
  
IV 
All of the above with CPR, adrenaline, defibrillation and ECMO as available 
 
Dr M Wu / Dr R Gihwala CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020 
Contents

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ACTIVELY HUNT FOR THE CAUSE 
 
*At risk population – elderly and infants 
*Hypoglycaemia 
*SEPSIS (always part of differential in extreme of age) 
*Intoxication 
*Hypothyroidism 
*Adrenal insufficiency 
*Malnutrition 
*Trauma 
*Elderly with co-morbidities 
*Burns 
*Shock 
*Environment 
*Iatrogenic (be cautious with fluid and blood products) 
 
 
Beware of diagnosing death in a hypothermic 
patient because hypothermia itself may 
produce a very slow, small-volume, irregular 
pulse and unrecordable blood pressure. 
 
Use ultrasound to check for cardiac activity 
No activity – patient likely demised 
Cardiac activity – patient must be warmed to 
32°C before declaring death 
CPR GUIDELINES VARY IN HYPOTHERMIA 
ALWAYS LOOK FOR TRAUMA IN DEPR
